Do not depend on ENABLE_PERSISTENT_CONFIG. Use threshold 30000 and cap 30000, CONTEXT_COMPACTION_MODEL set to the exact model id of the Gemma no-think task model (it must exist in the models list, or the chat model is used silently), and per-model compact_token_threshold=20000 for Pro. If the forced mid-loop test produces a template error in the vLLM logs, raise the threshold so compaction only triggers at turn start (above the largest single-turn deep-research size).

kept.title: Cap tool outputs at the source (deep research, page fetch, search) so the current turn stays small across hops
kept.what_to_change:
Within one turn, every tool hop re-sends all earlier tool results; the prefix is cached, but decode attention depth and the model's attention budget still grow. In the custom tools, return compact text instead of raw pages:
- page_fetch: main-content extraction (trafilatura or readability) cut to about 4,000 chars, plus title and URL.
- deep_research (8 pages in parallel): about 2,000-2,500 chars per page and about 16,000 chars total. Better: score paragraphs by keyword overlap with the query (or with the bge-m3 embedding already on :11435) and return the top 3-4 paragraphs per page with the source URL.
- search: return only title, URL and snippet (top 5-6), not page bodies.
- Playwright: return text and at most 1 screenshot per call. Each screenshot is about 1.1k+ soft tokens at max_soft_tokens 1120, plus vision encoder time.
Do NOT turn on ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH (0.12's deferred tool schemas). It saves a little schema text but adds a search_tools hop to every tool use, which costs more than it saves on a 4B-active model with about 8 tools, and it may make Gemma skip tools even more.
kept.expected_gain: A deep-research turn's context could fall from about 15-25k to about 5-7k tokens. That saves about 2-5 s of prefill at Spark rates (about 4-5k tok/s at 8-16k depth) on the hop that receives the results, keeps decode near the 50+ tok/s shallow-context regime for the final answer, and gives the model less irrelevant text to drift into. The effect on invented numbers is plausible but unproven.
evidence: https://docs.openwebui.com/features/extensibility/plugin/functions/filter.md (each tool hop passes the whole conversation through again)
https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/46tok-s-with-redhatai-gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-nvfp4/366005 (prefill and decode slow down with depth on Spark)
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-webui/open-webui/v0.12.0/backend/open_webui/config.py (ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH / TOOL_SEARCH_DEFER_THRESHOLD exist; default off)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Changes are only in your own Open WebUI tool Python, so no engine restart is needed. It also helps the Telegram bot if it shares the tools. bge-m3 is already running, so paragraph ranking adds about 50-150 ms per call on Ollama, but plain keyword scoring is effectively free.
kept.risk: Low to medium: aggressive cuts can drop the one paragraph holding the answer. Start with generous caps and check on your Uzbek eval set.
kept.test_plan: Run 5 deep-research prompts from your Uzbek eval before and after. Record prompt_tokens of the final hop, wall-clock time (target 10-20 s faster on 60-90 s runs) and answer correctness against known facts. Run 5 page-fetch Q&A prompts the same way. About 15 minutes.
kept.verifier_reason: This only touches the user's own tool code: no engine restart, no memory risk, and it helps the Telegram bot too. Deep research is already capped at 20s of time but not in characters, so this is not done yet. Smaller tool payloads cut prefill on the hop that receives them and keep decode in the shallow-context range. The gain is plausible for one user. Config check: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH exists (default False) and TOOL_SEARCH_DEFER_THRESHOLD defaults to 400. Leaving it off is correct for about 8 tools on a 4B-active model.
kept.corrected_change: Start generous: page_fetch about 6000 chars, deep_research about 3000 per page and 20000 total, with keyword/BM25 paragraph ranking first (it is free) and bge-m3 reranking only if quality drops. Always keep numbers and tables found in the top paragraphs. Leave ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH off.

kept.title: Add a per-request prefix-cache and prompt-size monitor so every context change is measured, not guessed
kept.what_to_change: vLLM 0.31 exposes counters vllm:prefix_cache_queries and vllm:prefix_cache_hits (in tokens, per engine) on /metrics, and it already logs a 'Prefix cache hit rate' periodically. Add a small script on the Spark, for example ~/bin/pc.sh: `curl -s localhost:${1:-8000}/metrics | grep -E '^vllm:prefix_cache_(queries|hits)_total|^vllm:prompt_tokens_total'`. Run it before and after each test message; delta hits / delta queries is the cache ratio for that turn. Optionally, extend the recommendation 1 filter with an outlet() that logs len(json.dumps(body['messages'])) and the number of images per request to the Open WebUI log, so prompt growth can be seen per chat. Optionally lower vLLM's periodic stats interval with --log-stats if it is off (it is on by default in the server).
kept.expected_gain: No direct speedup. It makes recommendations 1-4 verifiable in under a minute each and catches future regressions, for example a new tool or a system-prompt variable silently breaking the cache, which can cost 3-20 s per turn.
evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/v0.31.0/vllm/v1/metrics/loggers.py (counter names vllm:prefix_cache_queries / vllm:prefix_cache_hits, token-denominated)
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/v0.31.0/vllm/engine/arg_utils.py (--enable-prefix-caching, --prefix-caching-hash-algo, --mm-processor-cache-gb flags present in 0.31)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Works on both engines (:8000 Gemma, :8001 Qwen3.8). Prometheus counters get a _total suffix in exposition; if grep finds nothing, grep 'prefix_cache' without the suffix. MTP draft-model caching is separate and not shown in these counters.
kept.risk: None (read-only).
kept.test_plan: Run pc.sh, send 'salom' in a new chat, run pc.sh, send a second message in the same chat, and run pc.sh again. The second delta should show hits of at least the system prompt plus tools plus the first exchange. If hits stay near the system-prompt length only, the prefix is being broken (see recommendation 1). About 3 minutes.
kept.verifier_reason: It is read-only and useful for checking recommendations 1-4. The vLLM v1 counters vllm:prefix_cache_queries and vllm:prefix_cache_hits (in tokens) are exposed with the _total suffix, and vllm:prompt_tokens_total exists. One error: vLLM has no '--log-stats' flag. Stats logging is on by default and is turned off with --disable-log-stats. To change the interval, use VLLM_LOG_STATS_INTERVAL (env, default 10s).
kept.corrected_change: pc.sh: curl -s localhost:${1:-8000}/metrics | grep -E '^vllm:(prefix_cache_(queries|hits)|prompt_tokens)_total'. Drop the '--log-stats' suggestion. Make sure --disable-log-stats is not set, and if needed set VLLM_LOG_STATS_INTERVAL=5 on the container. Put the outlet() logging in a separate filter, or wrap it in try/except.

kept.title: Measure the real prefix-cache hit rate first (per request and global), because Gemma4 hybrid-SWA + MTP has had 0%-hit bugs
kept.what_to_change: Add `--enable-prompt-tokens-details` to the Gemma (:8000) and Qwen (:8001) serve commands so every response's usage carries `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. No other flag change is needed. Then read the engine counters: `curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep -E 'vllm:prefix_cache_(queries|hits)_total|vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc'`. The periodic engine log line also prints 'Prefix cache hit rate'. Also grep the startup log for 'GPU KV cache size' (tokens), 'max_num_batched_tokens' and any 'Disabling fine-grained prefix-cache hits' or prefix-caching warnings. If a cache-friendly flow (same chat, turn 2+) shows hits well below roughly 80-90% of prompt tokens, compare against the known bugs (#40624, #44082, #48435). Run an A/B with `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager` (needs more KV memory, so it may also need a lower --max-model-len) or with speculative decoding temporarily off, to see whether MTP is what breaks hits.
kept.expected_gain: Diagnostic. This step decides whether recs 2-4 are worth seconds or milliseconds. In the cited issues, fixing a broken prefix cache took warm TTFT at about 10k tokens from 2.24 s down to 0.81 s, and hit rates went from 0% to 81-91%.
evidence: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40624 (Gemma4 + hybrid attention + DFlash: 0% prefix hits; ~89% with --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager; ~91% without spec decode)
https://github.com/1CatAI/1Cat-vLLM/pull/657 (backport of upstream vllm#44082, merged 2026-06-02: SWA group + EAGLE/MTP speculation => prefix cache never hit)
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48435 (Gemma-4-31B hybrid-SWA prefix reuse collapsing to 0; fixed by #43447 + #52216, --prefix-cache-retention-interval default 0)
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53786 (SWA groups disable fine-grained prefix hits; open as of vLLM 0.30; MTP drafts without SWA group kept 93-98% hits)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Gemma 4 26B mixes sliding-window and full-attention layers, so vLLM uses the hybrid KV cache manager. Adding the MTP assistant drafter is exactly the combination where several 2026 bugs dropped hits to 0. vLLM 0.31 should already include the #44082, #43447 and #52216 fixes (all merged by Aug 2026). That is an inference from merge dates, not verified against the 0.31 release notes, so measure. --enable-prompt-tokens-details is a long-standing vLLM OpenAI-server flag. The counter names are the V1 metric names; confirm with grep, since the suffix may differ.
kept.risk: Very low: an observability flag only. The --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager A/B uses more KV memory for SWA layers. Run it only with --max-model-len lowered (e.g. 65536), and keep gpu-memory-utilization at 0.35 so the >=15 GiB free margin is kept.
kept.test_plan: (1) Restart Gemma with the flag. (2) Snapshot /metrics. (3) In one Open WebUI chat, send a plain question, then a follow-up, then a web-search question, then a follow-up. (4) Snapshot /metrics again and compute delta hits / delta queries. Also curl one request twice with the same 8k prompt and compare usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens and TTFT. Turn 2+ of a plain chat should show cached_tokens of about 90% or more of prompt_tokens. Takes about 10 minutes.
kept.verifier_reason: Valid and cheap. --enable-prompt-tokens-details is a long-standing vLLM OpenAI-server flag. vllm:prefix_cache_queries and vllm:prefix_cache_hits are V1 counters, and Prometheus adds _total. --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager exists. The Gemma4 hybrid-SWA plus MTP 0%-hit bug class is real and matches this stack (MTP drafter plus SWA). Whether 0.31 contains the fixes is unverified, which is why the step is a measurement. Gemma's measured 0.15-0.25s TTFT at 3.5k tokens suggests hits already work for the static prefix, but that does not prove turn-2+ or tool rounds hit. Two caveats. First, prefix-cache-retention is controlled through the VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL env var (per PR #45845), so do not add it as a CLI flag. Second, the --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager A/B must lower max-model-len and keep util at 0.35, as the recommendation already says.
kept.corrected_change: Add --enable-prompt-tokens-details to both serve commands. Read the counters with grep -E 'vllm:prefix_cache_(queries|hits)'. The suffix may or may not be _total. Do not pass a --prefix-cache-retention-interval flag; if needed, it is the env var VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL. Run the A/B with --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager --max-model-len 65536 at util 0.35, and also with --speculative-config removed.

kept.title: Stop Open WebUI from rewriting the cached prefix on tool rounds: turn off the Citations capability and system-prompt memory injection, and keep only static text in the system prompt
kept.what_to_change: In Open WebUI 0.12, change three things. (a) Admin Panel > Settings > Models > [Sarob, Sarob Tez, Pro] > Capabilities: untick 'Citations'. Put the citation rule into the static Uzbek system prompt, e.g. 'Manbalarni havola (URL) bilan keltir'; numbered [1] pills stop working, so cite by link. (b) Set env `ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT=false` (or Admin > Settings > General > Memory System Context off). The model can still recall through the memory tools under native function calling. Alternatively, keep it on but accept a miss whenever memories change; MEMORIES_CONTEXT_CHAR_LIMIT/MEMORIES_USER_CHAR_LIMIT cap its size. (c) Keep 'File Context' off and use File Upload + builtin Files tools instead, and keep the enabled tool list identical across turns (no per-chat tool toggling).
kept.expected_gain: Open WebUI's docs say that with Citations on, every tool round that returns sources rewrites both the system message and the last user message, so the whole prompt is re-prefilled each round. At 6-15k tokens and about 3-6k tok/s, that is roughly 1-5 s per round. A 3-4 round web-search answer could save about 3-15 s (the current 20-60 s range); deep research saves the most. Disabling memory context also stops misses after every memory update.
evidence: https://docs.openwebui.com/features/chat-conversations/prompt-caching (cache-breaker table: Citations re-applies RAG template into system message + rewrites last user message after tool rounds; Memory 'high impact'; ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT=false; checklist)
https://docs.openwebui.com/features/chat-conversations/memory (ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT default True; memory tools still work when off; MEMORIES_CONTEXT_CHAR_LIMIT / MEMORIES_USER_CHAR_LIMIT)
https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/gemma-4-day-1-inference-on-nvidia-dgx-spark-preliminary-benchmarks/365503 (26B-A4B pp2048 ~3105 tok/s on Spark)

https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/measured-inference-benchmarks-on-a-single-dgx-spark-same-harness-across-ollama-llama-cpp-and-vllm-notes-data-published/379766 (~6000 tok/s prefill, 27k prompt in 3.6 s)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: We use native function calling with custom tools (search, fetch, deep-research), and those tools return sources, which is exactly the documented breaker. Memory is on. The doc is written for hosted-provider caching, but vLLM APC has the same exact-prefix rule. Caveat: I did not verify in the 0.12 source whether custom (non-builtin) tools that emit sources trigger the rewrite the same way as builtin web search. Rec 1's metrics will show it.
kept.risk: UX: no clickable source pills under answers. Quality: personal facts are no longer always in context, and the model must call the memory tool. Gemma sometimes skips tools, so add a system-prompt line such as 'Foydalanuvchi haqida savol bo'lsa avval xotira vositasini chaqir'. Revert per item if the Uzbek eval drops.
kept.test_plan: Use the same scripted web-search question (e.g. today's USD/UZS rate plus 1 follow-up). Run it 3 times before and 3 times after the change. Record end-to-end time, TTFT per round (Open WebUI usage info or vLLM log), and the metrics delta from rec 1. Success means turn-2+ and tool-round hit rates above 80% and lower total latency. Takes about 15 minutes.
kept.verifier_reason: Confirmed in the Open WebUI docs. The prompt-caching page lists Citations as a very-high-impact breaker: after each tool round that returns sources, it re-applies the RAG template and source list to the system message and the last user message. It lists Memory system context as high impact, and File Context as high. The memory page confirms ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT (env var, default True), the admin toggle at Admin > Settings > General > Memory System Context (shown only when Memories is on), MEMORIES_CONTEXT_CHAR_LIMIT (default 2000) and MEMORIES_USER_CHAR_LIMIT. Memory tools keep working under native FC. This applies directly, since native FC is used with source-emitting search, fetch and deep-research tools. The size of the gain depends on whether the custom tools emit source events, so check that with rec 1. The quality risk is that Gemma skips tool calls, so keep the system-prompt nudge and run the Uzbek eval.
kept.corrected_change: Make each change separately and A/B each one. Test Citations off first, since it has the biggest effect. If the custom tools do not emit sources/citation events, this change gives no gain for them.

kept.title: Move all per-request varying tokens (date/time, user-context) out of the system prompt into the tail of the last user message, and make the Telegram bot prefix byte-identical
kept.what_to_change: (a) Check the Sarob system prompt(s) for `{{CURRENT_TIME}}`, `{{CURRENT_DATETIME}}`, `{{CURRENT_WEEKDAY}}` or `{{CURRENT_TIMEZONE}}`. Remove them, or keep at most `{{CURRENT_DATE}}`, which changes once a day. (b) If the model needs the time, either rely on the native `get_current_timestamp` builtin tool, or add a tiny Open WebUI Filter function whose `inlet(body)` appends e.g. `\n\n[Hozirgi vaqt: 2026-10-13 14:05, Toshkent]` to the content of the LAST user message only. The system prompt and tool specs then stay a byte-identical prefix. (c) In the Telegram bot agent loop, build the system prompt once at startup with no timestamps, user names or counters at the top. Serialize the tool list in a fixed order, e.g. `json.dumps(tools, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False)` in a constant list order, and never re-order or re-filter tools between rounds. Append new messages only; never edit earlier messages, and put retrieved context into the newest user or tool message.
kept.expected_gain: A time-of-day variable at the top of the prompt makes every request a full cold prefill of 1.8k system + tools + history. For a 10k-token chat that is about 2-3 s versus about 0.2 s TTFT. For the bot, every tool round of an agent loop goes from cold to about 95% cached.
evidence: https://docs.openwebui.com/features/chat-conversations/chat-features/temporal-awareness (nothing is injected unless placeholders are used; CURRENT_TIME/CURRENT_DATETIME definitions; get_current_timestamp tool under native FC)
https://docs.openwebui.com/features/chat-conversations/prompt-caching (static system prompt; cache invalidated from the first differing token to the end)
https://docs.fireworks.ai/guides/prompt-caching.md (dynamic content/timestamps at start of system prompt is a common cache mistake; place at end)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: This applies to any vLLM APC deployment. It matters more for Gemma 4 under the hybrid manager, because a mismatch early in the prompt also discards the SWA tail blocks. Open WebUI Filter functions with `inlet` are a standard 0.12 extension point. Uzbek has no special impact, but keep the injected tag short and fixed-format.
kept.risk: Low. The model sees the time later in the context, which is arguably better for recency. A Filter that mutates history instead of only the last message would itself break the cache, so only append to body['messages'][-1].
kept.test_plan: In one chat, send 3 messages 2 minutes apart. Compare `cached_tokens` and TTFT before and after removing time variables; turn 3 should show cached_tokens of at least prompt_tokens minus the new message. For the bot, log usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens per round of a 3-tool task. Takes about 10 minutes.
kept.verifier_reason: This is sound exact-prefix APC hygiene. Open WebUI only injects time when a template placeholder ({{CURRENT_TIME}}, {{CURRENT_DATETIME}}, etc.) is used, so this is a check-then-fix item; it may already be fine. Inlet filters that append to body['messages'][-1] are a standard extension point. The Telegram bot advice (static system prompt, fixed tool order, append-only history) is correct and probably the largest win for the bot's agent loop. One caveat: a time tag appended to the last user message persists in history only if the filter's mutation is saved. Otherwise later turns differ from what was cached at the earlier turn's tail, which costs only the one latest message. That is acceptable.

kept.title: Raise --max-num-batched-tokens to 16384 on the Gemma engine for faster cold prefill and image-heavy prompts
kept.what_to_change: First grep the Gemma startup log for the resolved `max_num_batched_tokens`; the V1 default depends on usage context and device memory and is 2048 or 8192. If it is below 16384, add `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384` to the Gemma command and leave --max-num-seqs 8 unchanged. Do not touch Qwen first; it is dense and slower and is better tested separately. Leave chunked prefill on (the V1 default).
kept.expected_gain: A cold 15k-token prompt runs in 1 step instead of 2 (or 8 at 2048). Larger GEMM batches use the MoE and FP4 kernels better. Expect about 5-15% faster cold prefill, more if the current value is 2048. With 11-32 images at about 1120 soft tokens each, the encoder budget per step grows, so the screenshot-to-Excel and many-image prompts (up to 50k tokens) should see the biggest TTFT cut. These are estimates; there is no Spark-specific published A/B.
evidence: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization/ (higher max_num_batched_tokens => better TTFT; smaller => better ITL; >8192 recommended for throughput on large GPUs)

https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/gemma-4-day-1-inference-on-nvidia-dgx-spark-preliminary-benchmarks/365503 (prefill tok/s still rising from pp512 1299 to pp2048 3105 => larger chunks are more efficient on GB10)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: With a single user, there is almost never a concurrent decode stream whose ITL a big prefill chunk would hurt. The exception is Telegram and Open WebUI running at the same moment, which is rare. The flag name is valid in vLLM 0.31. The encoder cache budget follows max_num_batched_tokens or the largest mm item. That is from my knowledge of vLLM internals and was not re-verified in 0.31 source.
kept.risk: A larger profiling peak activation lowers the KV pool slightly at the same 0.35 utilization; check that 'GPU KV cache size' is still far above 131072 tokens. A concurrent decode stream may stutter briefly during a 16k prefill. Keep free memory above 15 GiB (watch `free -g` during an image-heavy request).
kept.test_plan: Use a fixed cold prompt with a unique random first line to defeat the cache: about 15k tokens of Uzbek text, plus a separate 11-screenshot request. Measure TTFT with streaming curl 3 times each at the current value and at 16384, and compare medians. Also run one normal chat to confirm decode tok/s is unchanged. Takes about 15 minutes, including one restart.
kept.verifier_reason: The flag is valid, and a larger chunk helps single-user cold TTFT. The gain is overstated, though. On a GPU reporting more than about 70 GB (GB10 reports about 120 GB), the V1 API-server default is very likely already 8192, so the step is 8192 to 16384. That saves one extra scheduler step per 8k tokens, which is probably a few percent (roughly 0.1-0.3s on a 15k cold prompt), not 5-15%. For multimodal models the encoder budget is already at least the largest single mm item, so image-heavy gains are uncertain. A larger profiling activation peak at fixed util 0.35 shrinks the KV pool. It is low risk and testable, so keep it as a low-priority A/B, and only after rec 1 and rec 2. Most prompts should be cache hits anyway, which makes cold prefill matter less.
kept.corrected_change: First read the resolved max_num_batched_tokens from the startup log. If it is 8192, expect only a marginal gain and test --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 as a low-priority A/B. Keep gpu-memory-utilization at 0.35 and confirm that 'GPU KV cache size' stays far above 131072 tokens.

kept.title: Do NOT add LMCache or native CPU KV offloading on GB10; size the GPU KV pool from metrics instead
kept.what_to_change: Skip `--kv-offloading-backend native|lmcache --kv-offloading-size N` and the OffloadingConnector `--kv-transfer-config`. On GB10 'CPU' and 'GPU' are the same LPDDR5x, so offloading just copies KV within the same 273 GB/s memory, and its pinned buffer counts against the same 121 GiB. Act only if rec 1 shows `vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc` near 1.0 or cached chats dropping out after a few hours. If so, raise Gemma `--gpu-memory-utilization` by 0.02-0.03 (e.g. 0.35 -> 0.38, about +3.6 GiB of KV) and keep at least 15 GiB free. Leave `--prefix-cache-retention-interval` at its default 0. It keeps the latest prompt boundary per request, which is what multi-turn chat and tool loops need, and costs no capacity for running requests.
kept.expected_gain: Avoids weeks of unprofitable experimentation and memory risk. With fp8 KV and SWA layers bounded to a 1024-token window, the current about 20 GiB Gemma KV pool most likely already holds several hundred thousand tokens. That is enough for one user's active chats. This is an estimate; confirm with the 'GPU KV cache size' log line.
evidence: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-10-tiered-kv-offloading (tiered offloading via --kv-transfer-config / cpu_bytes_to_use; benchmarks are multi-request throughput on H100, no single-user latency)
https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-01-08-kv-offloading-connector (native CPU backend; --kv_offloading_backend native --kv_offloading_size)
https://docs.vultr.com/inference-cookbook/rocm/optimization/kv-cache-offloading (with large device memory offloading is often unnecessary; some models need --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager)
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48435 (offload was only a workaround for SWA collapse under memory pressure; real fix = prefix-cache retention, default 0 since #52216)
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52216 (--prefix-cache-retention-interval: 0 default = latest replayable boundary; N = every N tokens; None = every block)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: This is specific to unified memory. The discrete-GPU benefit (cheap host RAM behind PCIe) does not exist on GB10, and the box has frozen before when memory fractions went too high. Offload connectors historically disabled the hybrid manager, which would waste memory on Gemma's SWA layers.
kept.risk: The recommendation itself carries no risk. Raising gpu-memory-utilization is the only risky action; change it by 0.02-0.03 at most and watch `free -g`.
kept.test_plan: Read 'GPU KV cache size: N tokens' in the startup log and vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc after a normal day of use. If usage stays below 0.7 and hits stay high in rec 1, do nothing. Takes about 5 minutes.
kept.verifier_reason: The reasoning is correct. On unified LPDDR5x, CPU offload copies KV within the same memory pool, uses up the same 121 GiB budget and adds freeze risk. Offload connectors have historically needed the hybrid manager disabled, which wastes memory on SWA layers. For one user, a GPU KV pool of about 20 GiB with fp8 KV and SWA layers is ample. Small correction: the retention interval is set through the env var VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL (PR #45845), not necessarily a CLI flag. In any case the advice is to leave it unset, which is fine. The claim that it 'costs no capacity' is unverified, so drop it.
kept.corrected_change: Do not set any retention option; leave the default. If metrics later show kv_cache_usage_perc near 1.0, raise Gemma util by at most 0.02-0.03 and check that free -g stays at 15 GiB or more.

kept.title: Make the screenshot->Excel tool fan out: one vLLM request per image, in parallel, thinking off, TSV output
kept.what_to_change: In the image-table-to-Excel tool, stop sending all 11 images in one chat turn. For each image, POST its own /v1/chat/completions to Gemma on :8000 with asyncio.gather and a semaphore of 6. Keep 2 of the 8 max-num-seqs slots free for chat. Request body: temperature 0, max_tokens 4096, thinking disabled with chat_template_kwargs {"enable_thinking": false} (or the gemma4 equivalent your reasoning-config uses), and a fixed short system prompt so the prefix cache hits. Prompt: 'Transcribe the table exactly. Output TSV only: one row per line, tab-separated, first line = header. No commentary, no markdown, keep numbers exactly as shown (spaces/commas/decimal separators), empty cell = empty.' Parse the TSV in Python with openpyxl, merge the pages, and convert numeric cells using Uzbek/Russian formats ('1 234,56'). Stop asking the LLM to emit JSON or markdown tables: pipes and quotes waste about 20-40% of output tokens.
kept.expected_gain: Estimate: 11 screenshots drop from 30-60 s to about 8-15 s. Single-stream decode is about 50 tok/s, and aggregate throughput at batch 6 on a ~4B-active MoE is usually 3-5x higher, because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and the weights are shared across the batch. Turning thinking off removes up to 512 tokens per image. TSV saves a further 20-40% of output tokens. Accuracy should be the same or better, since each image gets the model's full attention instead of 11 images x 1120 = 12k vision tokens in one context.
evidence: https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/recipes/en/stable/Google/Gemma4.html (per-image soft-token budgets 70-1120; higher = more compute)
https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-01-vllm-dgx-spark (GB10 unified-memory, bandwidth-bound decode)
Operator measurement in context: MTP acceptance ~3.3 tokens; max-num-seqs 8 already configured
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Uses only the existing Gemma endpoint and the max-num-seqs 8 already configured, so it adds no memory. MTP speculative decoding still works under batching, though acceptance gains shrink somewhat at batch 6. This is a code change in the Open WebUI tool and changes no server flags.
kept.risk: Low. Parallel jobs briefly compete with live chat. Keep the semaphore at 6 or below. With thinking off, tables with merged headers are slightly more likely to be misread. The per-image prompt mitigates this, and if needed you can re-run a single image with thinking on.
kept.test_plan: Take the same 11 screenshots you already used. (a) Time the current flow. (b) Time the fan-out version with semaphore 1, 4 and 6, and log the summed completion_tokens. Compare cell accuracy by diffing the resulting xlsx files against a hand-checked ground truth for 2-3 images (count wrong cells). Watch vLLM /metrics vllm:num_requests_running and the generation throughput log line. About 10 min.
kept.verifier_reason: This only changes the tool, so it adds no memory, and max-num-seqs 8 is already set. Batched decode on a bandwidth-bound MoE with about 4B active parameters gives several times more aggregate tok/s, and per-image requests avoid a 12k-token vision context. TSV and thinking-off also cut output tokens. The 3-5x aggregate figure is optimistic: MTP acceptance and its gains fall at batch 6, and six concurrent 1120-token image prefills compete with live chat TTFT. A realistic target is about 2-3x. Two further issues: (1) In vLLM, Gemma 4 thinking is controlled by chat_template_kwargs enable_thinking. Confirm that the deployed template honours enable_thinking=false, or that skip_special_tokens/reasoning parser output comes back empty. (2) The text-only system-prompt prefix still hits the cache, but image tokens differ per request.
kept.corrected_change: Use asyncio.gather with Semaphore(4), not 6, so prefill bursts don't stall chat; test 4 against 6. Send extra_body {"chat_template_kwargs":{"enable_thinking":false}, "temperature":0, "max_tokens":4096} and verify there is no reasoning_content in the response. Use TSV output parsed with openpyxl and Uzbek/Russian number normalisation (NBSP, thin space, comma decimal). Keep the text in cells as strings when a value is ambiguous, for example codes with leading zeros.

kept.title: Keep 1120 as the server default; drop to 560 or 280 per request for non-OCR images
kept.what_to_change: Keep --mm-processor-kwargs '{"max_soft_tokens":1120}' for the main server. 1120 is the maximum, and the vLLM recipe says higher budgets give more detail, which dense tables need. For the chat models where most images are photos rather than documents (Sarob Tez, Telegram bot), send the vLLM extra field "mm_processor_kwargs": {"max_soft_tokens": 280} or 560 per request. In Open WebUI 0.12 use Workspace > Models > Advanced Params > custom parameter. In the Telegram bot, add it to the request body. I could not confirm from current docs that the OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint accepts per-request mm_processor_kwargs for Gemma 4; check vllm/entrypoints/openai protocol in 0.31. If it is rejected, keep the server default.
kept.expected_gain: Each photo goes from 1120 to 280 vision tokens, about 4x fewer image tokens. A 50k-token many-image request would shrink to roughly 15-20k, cutting prefill and vision-encoder time by about 50-70% and freeing KV. There is no OCR loss, because the table tool keeps 1120.
evidence: https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/recipes/en/stable/Google/Gemma4.html (supported 70/140/280/560/1120, default 280, server-wide via --mm-processor-kwargs)
https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it/discussions/51 (community discussion on raising the default to 1120)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Gemma 4 on vLLM 0.31 with the processor kwarg you already set. Uncertainty: per-request override support on the OpenAI server path for this model.
kept.risk: Low-medium. If the override is silently ignored you get no gain and no harm. Using 280 on screenshots of text would hurt OCR, so apply it only to the photo/chat paths.
kept.test_plan: Send one 50k-style multi-image request with and without extra_body mm_processor_kwargs max_soft_tokens=280. Compare usage.prompt_tokens: it should fall sharply if the override works, and if it doesn't change, the override is unsupported. Then compare TTFT. 5 min.
kept.verifier_reason: vLLM's ChatCompletionRequest has an mm_processor_kwargs extra field, so a per-request override is plausible. Gemma 4 supports budgets of 70-1120. Whether the Gemma4 processor actually applies max_soft_tokens per request in 0.31 is unverified; the prompt_tokens test proposed in the recommendation settles it in minutes. The main flaw is the assumption that chat or Telegram images are mostly photos. An Uzbek user often sends screenshots of documents, receipts or tables in chat, and 280 would hurt OCR there. A blanket per-model downgrade risks quality, which the goal forbids.
kept.corrected_change: Do not set the reduced budget model-wide. Apply it adaptively in an Open WebUI filter function (inlet) or in the Telegram bot: when a request has more than 4 images, set body["mm_processor_kwargs"]={"max_soft_tokens":560}, and keep 1120 for 4 or fewer images or when the user or tool intent is OCR/table. Verify the override with usage.prompt_tokens before relying on it. If prompt_tokens does not change, the override is unsupported, so drop this change.

kept.title: A/B a dedicated 0.9B document VLM (PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 first, GLM-OCR second) as a third small vLLM container used only by the Excel tool
kept.what_to_change: Run a separate container from the same image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0 serve PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 (or PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL if the 1.5 repo is not supported in 0.31) with --trust-remote-code --port 8002 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.06 --max-model-len 16384 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-num-seqs 8 --no-enable-prefix-caching --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --served-model-name paddleocr-vl. The client prompt is exactly 'Table Recognition:' with temperature 0. The output is HTML/OTSL-style table markup, which you parse to xlsx with pandas.read_html. Alternative: zai-org/GLM-OCR with --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":1}' and the prompt 'Table Recognition:'. It needs vLLM >= 0.16 and transformers >= 5, so it should work on 0.31. Prefer PaddleOCR-VL for Uzbek, because it advertises 100+ languages including Cyrillic and Latin scripts, while the GLM-OCR card lists only 8 languages without naming them. Keep Gemma as a fallback and as a validator: run a cheap Gemma pass to check the row and column count.
kept.expected_gain: Reported scores: PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 OmniDocBench v1.5 about 88 overall with table TEDS about 87 (aggregator figure). GLM-OCR claims 94.6 overall and 0.67 images/s single-concurrency on its own hardware. A 0.9B dense model should decode several times faster than Gemma's MoE plus MTP on GB10's ~273 GB/s, so plausibly 1-3 s per screenshot. These are unverified on GB10. The main expected benefit is fewer misread digits on dense numeric tables, not just speed.
evidence: https://recipes.vllm.ai/PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL (serve flags, task prompts, recommends disabling prefix cache and mm cache for OCR)
https://recipes.vllm.ai/zai-org/GLM-OCR (MTP 1 token, vLLM 0.16+, transformers 5)
https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-OCR (OmniDocBench v1.5 94.62, 0.67 img/s)
https://benchmarklist.com/models/z-ai-glm-ocr/ and https://www.codesota.com/ocr/benchmark/olmocr-bench (aggregated olmOCR-bench / OmniDocBench numbers, secondary sources)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: About 2 GB of weights in BF16. At util 0.06 (~7 GB) it fits within your ≥15 GiB free rule only if you check free memory first: current usage is 0.35 + 0.28 + Ollama + Open WebUI. If headroom is tight, start it on demand (docker start / stop inside the tool) or stop the idle Qwen3.6 if it is loaded. GB10 sm_121 support for these small Qwen2-style or ERNIE-style towers under vLLM 0.31 is unconfirmed; I found no GB10 report. Expect Triton or FlashInfer attention fallbacks, as you saw with Gemma.
kept.risk: Medium. Possible remote-code or transformers-version incompatibility in the 0.31 image. The output format differs from Gemma's, so the parser needs work. Adding a third engine raises the risk of freezing the box, so set util explicitly and never rely on autotune. Uzbek-specific accuracy, such as o' and g' with apostrophes, is untested.
kept.test_plan: Before starting, run free -g and confirm at least 22 GiB free. Start the container (about 2 GB download, roughly 5 min at your link speed). Run the same 3 ground-truth screenshots through it and through Gemma at 1120, and record per-image latency and wrong-cell count. Only adopt it if wrong cells are equal or lower and latency is at least 2x lower. Under 15 min after the download.
kept.verifier_reason: vLLM supports PaddleOCR-VL natively (PaddleOCRVLForConditionalGeneration, since about 0.11) and GLM-OCR (0.16+), and the flags (--mm-processor-cache-gb, --no-enable-prefix-caching, --max-num-seqs) exist. A 0.9B model decodes much faster than Gemma. Corrections: (1) PaddleOCR-VL's 'Table Recognition:' prompt emits OTSL tokens (<fcel>, <ecel>, <nl> and so on), not HTML, so pandas.read_html will not parse it. You need an OTSL-to-grid converter, such as the one in PaddleX/PaddleOCR. GLM-OCR does output HTML tables. (2) A third resident vLLM engine on the 121 GiB box is risky: CUDA context, torch.compile and graphs add several GB on top of util 0.06. sm_121 support for these vision towers is unverified. This is acceptable only as an on-demand A/B experiment, not as a permanently running service.
kept.corrected_change: Treat this as an experiment only. Before starting, check free -g for at least 25 GiB. Run: docker run ... vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0 --model PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL --trust-remote-code --port 8002 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.06 --max-model-len 16384 --max-num-seqs 8 --no-enable-prefix-caching --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --enforce-eager. Use --enforce-eager on the first run to avoid compile memory spikes. Parse the OTSL output into rows (<fcel>/<ecel> = cell, <nl> = row end), or try GLM-OCR, whose HTML table output does work with pandas.read_html. Adopt it only if wrong cells are less than or equal to Gemma's and latency is at least 2x lower. If adopted, start and stop the container on demand rather than keeping it resident.

kept.title: Pre-process screenshots in the tool: crop to the table and split tall images instead of downscaling
kept.what_to_change: In the tool, before sending: (1) trim uniform borders and UI chrome with a PIL bbox on non-background pixels. (2) If the image is taller than about 2x its width (long scrolled tables), split it into overlapping horizontal strips of about 1.3 MP with an overlap of 1-2 rows, and send each as its own parallel request (see rec 1). Then de-duplicate the overlapping rows by exact match. (3) Do not upscale crisp screenshots. Upscale ×2 with LANCZOS only when the text height is under about 10 px. Gemma's 1120 budget corresponds to roughly 2.5 MP; anything larger is downsampled and small digits blur.
kept.expected_gain: Fewer digit errors on long or dense tables, plus better parallelism: more, smaller requests finish sooner under batching. Expected: wrong cells near zero on screenshots that currently fail. It costs about 50 ms of CPU per image.
evidence: https://aiweekly.co/alerts/google-space-demos-gemma-4s-tunable-vision-token-budget (1120 ≈ max detail, about 2.5 MP)
https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/recipes/en/stable/Google/Gemma4.html
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Pure Python with PIL in the Open WebUI tool, with no server change. It works with either Gemma or a dedicated OCR model.
kept.risk: Low. Row de-duplication can fail if the same row legitimately appears twice. Use row index or overlap logic, not a global dedupe.
kept.test_plan: Pick the 2 worst-performing screenshots, such as a long scrolled table and a small font. Run them with and without crop and split, and count wrong cells and latency. 10 min.
kept.verifier_reason: This is pure PIL work in the tool. The 1120-token budget works out to roughly 2.5 MP (16px patches pooled 3x3, so about 48x48 px per soft token), which makes the downsampling-blur argument for tall scrolled tables sound. It costs negligible CPU and fits recommendation 1's per-request fan-out. The dedup caveat is correctly identified. Strips should not split a row, so overlap on whole rows.
kept.corrected_change: Only split when height > 2x width and total pixels > about 2.5 MP. Use an overlap of 1-2 row heights. Dedupe only the boundary rows between adjacent strips: compare the last k rows of strip i with the first k rows of strip i+1. Never dedupe globally.

kept.title: Add a deterministic verification pass so Gemma doesn't invent numbers in tables
kept.what_to_change: After the TSV comes back, check in Python: every row has the same column count, numeric columns parse, and any totals row equals the column sum where one exists. On failure, re-run only that image (or strip) once with thinking on, thinking_token_budget 512, and a prompt naming the failing row. Optionally run a cheap CPU OCR such as RapidOCR or PaddleOCR PP-OCRv5 on the aarch64 CPU to extract the digit strings only, and flag cells whose digits are absent from the CPU OCR output. Surface flagged cells to the user in yellow in the xlsx using an openpyxl PatternFill.
kept.expected_gain: This turns silent hallucinations into visible flags and fixes most structural errors with one targeted retry. The extra latency applies only on failures (+3-6 s), so the usual path is not slowed.
evidence: Context: observed issue 'Gemma sometimes ... invents numbers'
https://recipes.vllm.ai/PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL (greedy decoding recommended for OCR; same principle applies)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Tool-side only, so the server is untouched. A CPU OCR cross-check is optional; PP-OCRv5 or RapidOCR on ARM64 via onnxruntime is plausible but untested on Grace.
kept.risk: Low. False flags are possible with locale number formats, so normalise spaces, commas and NBSP before comparing.
kept.test_plan: Deliberately feed one blurry screenshot and confirm the validator flags or retries it. Then run the 11-image set and confirm the fast path adds less than 0.5 s total. 10 min.
kept.verifier_reason: Column-count, numeric-parse and totals checks run in microseconds, and retrying only the failing images adds latency just on failure. This directly targets the observed habit of inventing numbers. thinking_token_budget is already used by this stack. RapidOCR on aarch64 via onnxruntime is plausible but optional. Highlighting with openpyxl PatternFill is trivial. Normalise locale formats before any comparison.
kept.corrected_change: Keep the retry to one attempt per image, with enable_thinking true and thinking_token_budget 512. Run the optional CPU OCR digit cross-check in a thread pool so it overlaps the GPU calls, and enable it only if it adds less than 1 s for 11 images on Grace.

kept.title: Run the vLLM engines on the 10 Cortex-X925 cores and move Chromium, SearXNG, Open WebUI, Jupyter and Ollama to the A725 cores
kept.what_to_change: 1) Check the core layout first: `for c in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu[0-9]*; do echo $c $(cat $c/cpufreq/cpuinfo_max_freq); done`. One community runbook reports that on GB10 the big cores are 5-9 and 15-19 and the little cores are 0-4 and 10-14 (interleaved), so `taskset -c 0-9` would put a job only on little cores. Trust what your own sysfs shows over that mapping. 2) Gemma container: add `--cpuset-cpus=5-9,15-19` to `docker run`, or `cpuset: "5-9,15-19"` in compose. The Qwen :8001 container can share the same cores, because it is idle most of the time. 3) Open WebUI, the Playwright/Chromium browser tool (deep research opens 8 pages in parallel), SearXNG, Jupyter, the Open Terminal sandbox and the Ollama bge-m3 container: `--cpuset-cpus=0-4,10-14`. The Open WebUI CPU reranker also goes there. 4) Governor: `cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor`. If it is not `performance`, set it with `sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance`, or persist it with a systemd unit.
kept.expected_gain: Not measured on GB10 for vLLM, so this is an estimate. Single-stream decode of a ~4B-active MoE with MTP, at 50-60 tok/s, is partly bound by host-side work: the Python engine-core loop, sampling, spec-decode bookkeeping and detokenization. I expect 0-10% higher steady tok/s. The bigger gain should be removing tok/s drops and TTFT spikes while deep research or Playwright saturate the CPU. Those tool phases are exactly when the model is generating.
evidence: https://llama-cpp-ex.hexdocs.pm/dgx-spark.html (GB10 core map: big 5-9,15-19, little 0-4,10-14; p50 latency 21.5us on cpu19 vs 29.1us on cpu0)
https://daniel.lawrence.lu/blog/2026-07-15-dgx-spark-as-daily-driver/ (scheduler put work on slow A725 cores; pinning to X925 fixed it)
https://learn.arm.com/learning-paths/laptops-and-desktops/dgx_spark_llamacpp/1a_gb10_setup/
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Docker `--cpuset-cpus` works for vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0 and every other container. Open WebUI uses host networking, but cpuset still applies. The GPU kernels are not affected; this only takes CPU contention off vLLM's host loop. Caveat: Chromium on 10 little cores may make the page-fetch tools slightly slower (~10-20%), so compare total end-to-end time, not only tok/s.
kept.risk: Low. It can be undone with a container restart. If the core map is wrong for your unit, vLLM ends up on slow cores and gets worse, which is why step 1 is mandatory.
kept.test_plan: (~10 min) A: current setup. B: pinned. Each time run (a) 5x the same 6k-token prompt with max_tokens 512 against :8000 and read decode tok/s from vLLM logs or the /metrics `vllm:time_per_output_token_seconds`; (b) the same prompt while `stress-ng --cpu 10 --taskset 0-4,10-14` (or one deep-research query) runs in parallel. Keep B if tok/s under load is within 3% of the idle value and median/p90 TTFT does not get worse.

kept.title: Memory hygiene: headless mode, low swappiness, drop page cache before engine start, and size KV in fixed bytes instead of utilization fractions
kept.what_to_change: 1) Headless: `sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target` (reported to save 2-3 GB; GNOME plus daemons can hold more). 2) `/etc/sysctl.d/99-llm.conf`: `vm.swappiness=1` and `vm.dirty_bytes=268435456`, then `sudo sysctl --system`. Keep a small swap rather than none, unless you see swap-in during inference (`vmstat 1`, si/so columns); in that case run `swapoff -a`. Do not add zram: it compresses inside the same unified pool and takes memory from the GPU. 3) In the systemd unit or launch script, before the first engine starts: `ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c 'sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches'`. Run it once at start, never periodically. This is NVIDIA's documented GB10 workaround, because cudaMemGetInfo does not count reclaimable page cache (vLLM issue #35313). 4) Size KV deterministically with `--kv-cache-memory-bytes` (valid engine arg; description 'Size of KV Cache per GPU in bytes'). Read the current 'GPU KV cache size: N tokens' log line for each engine, then set e.g. Gemma `--kv-cache-memory-bytes 10G` and Qwen3.8 `--kv-cache-memory-bytes 6G`, adjusted so the log line still shows max concurrency >=2 at 131072. Keep `--gpu-memory-utilization` as the ceiling for the non-KV part. 5) Start order: the larger engine first, let it settle, check `/proc/meminfo` MemAvailable (nvidia-smi shows 'Not Supported' for memory on GB10), then start the second.
kept.expected_gain: No direct tok/s gain. It removes the cause of startup failures and box freezes, and it typically frees 5-15 GiB. That freed memory can pay for rec #3 (BF16 KV), more KV for Telegram-plus-WebUI overlap, or keeping a third model resident. Single-user KV utilization on Spark is reported below 5%, so both engines are probably over-reserving.
evidence: https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/known-issues.html (cudaMemGetInfo underreports reclaimable memory; drop_caches workaround; nvidia-smi memory Not Supported)
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/35313 (vLLM misreads free memory on GB10/GH200 UMA)

https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/memory-creep-on-dgx-spark-where-your-128-gb-actually-goes-and-how-to-stop-it/364886 (headless -2-3GB, swappiness=1, dirty_bytes=256MiB, warning: fastsafetensors + util>0.76 can freeze)
https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-01-vllm-dgx-spark (KV utilization <5% single user)

https://dev.to/ric03uec/two-qwen3-models-on-one-dgx-spark-the-residency-math-for-local-llm-coding-5bpj (two-engine residency: budget ~5 GiB overhead per process, load big first, keep sum of fractions <0.95)
https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/engine_args.html (--kv-cache-memory-bytes)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: All of these are standard Linux and vLLM 0.31 engine args. Gemma 4 uses hybrid sliding-window attention, so 131k context needs much less KV than a full-attention model, and the current 0.35 fraction (~42 GB) is probably far more than needed. Uncertainty: in some versions `--kv-cache-memory-bytes` bypasses the gpu_memory_utilization-based KV profiling. Confirm in the startup log that the KV size matches what you set.
kept.risk: Low to medium. Setting the KV bytes too low causes request queueing or preemption on 50k-token image prompts. Check the 'Maximum concurrency' log line. Headless mode removes the local desktop, which you can re-enable with graphical.target.
kept.test_plan: (~15 min) Record `grep -E 'MemAvailable|SwapFree' /proc/meminfo` and the two engines' KV log lines. Apply 1-3, reboot, start the engines with the KV-bytes flags, and record MemAvailable again (target: at least 25 GiB free with both engines and all services up). Run one 50k-token, 30-image request plus a parallel Telegram request and confirm there is no preemption warning in the logs and `vmstat 1` shows si/so=0.

kept.title: A/B test BF16 KV cache on Gemma (`--kv-cache-dtype auto`) instead of fp8, paid for by the memory freed in rec #2
kept.what_to_change: On the Gemma :8000 engine, change `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` to `--kv-cache-dtype auto` (BF16) and leave everything else unchanged, including the TRITON_ATTN backend and MTP 4. If memory is tight, cut max-model-len to 98304 for the test, or use the KV byte budget from rec #2.
kept.expected_gain: Uncertain; it has to be measured. The vLLM team's own DGX Spark guide says fp8 KV 'can carry a performance cost on Spark' and should be used only under memory pressure. With the Triton attention path, fp8 KV adds dequant work in prefill and decode. At your typical 6-15k context I would expect 0-8% better decode and slightly better TTFT on uncached prefill. It may also remove a small quality loss on long Uzbek contexts. If it is not faster, revert.
evidence: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-01-vllm-dgx-spark (avoid --kv-cache-dtype fp8 unless memory pressure requires it; it can carry a performance cost on Spark)
https://daniel.lawrence.lu/blog/2026-07-15-dgx-spark-as-daily-driver/ (counterpoint: NVFP4 KV improved TTFT on other models/backends)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: `--kv-cache-dtype auto` is valid in vLLM 0.31. Gemma 4's sliding-window layers keep BF16 KV at 131k affordable. The evidence is mixed: the Spark speedups people report for low-precision KV come from FlashInfer/TRT-LLM paths, while you are forced onto TRITON_ATTN, which is exactly where fp8 dequant overhead tends to show up. This is a test, not a sure win.
kept.risk: Low. Doubling KV memory could exceed the budget at 50k-token image prompts with several concurrent requests. Watch the KV log line and preemption warnings.
kept.test_plan: (~10 min, two engine restarts) Same harness as rec #1: 5x a 12k-token prompt with max_tokens 512, plus 3x a 30k prompt with prefix caching disabled per request (unique prefix), at temperature 0. Compare decode tok/s, TTFT and MTP acceptance rate (vLLM spec-decode metrics). Keep BF16 only if decode or TTFT is at least 3% better and memory headroom stays at or above 15 GiB.

kept.title: Check for thermal and power throttling; if present, cap GPU clocks around 2100 MHz with a persistent systemd unit and update DGX OS and firmware
kept.what_to_change: 1) Measure first: during a deep-research run plus the 11-screenshot Excel job, run `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,clocks.sm,power.draw,temperature.gpu,clocks_event_reasons.active --format=csv -l 1 > clk.csv`, and also `cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone*/temp`. 2) If you see SW/HW thermal slowdown bits, SoC zones above 90 C, or any past freeze or abrupt power-off, add `/etc/systemd/system/gpu-clock.service` with ExecStart=`nvidia-smi -pm 1` and `nvidia-smi -lgc 0,2100`, ExecStop=`nvidia-smi -rgc`, and enable it (lgc does not survive reboot). After setting it, read back the actual clock, because GB10 snaps to discrete steps. 3) Run `sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade` for DGX OS, plus `fwupdmgr refresh && fwupdmgr get-updates` for the platform firmware. A 2026 forum report says the system firmware update materially improved stability under sustained load. Make sure the unit has clear airflow and uses the supplied power brick.
kept.expected_gain: Decode tok/s stays nearly flat: on GB10 it is bandwidth-bound, and one 2026 measurement saw 51.3 tok/s uncapped vs 51.4 at 2200 MHz vs 50.7 at 1900 MHz. Prefill may drop ~2-5% at 2100 MHz (~14% at 1400 MHz). The benefit is ~15-20% lower power, cooler GPU, and no hard freezes or power-offs, which matters because you have frozen the box before. Do not cap if the measurement shows no throttling and the box has never frozen.

kept.applies_to_our_stack: Driver 580 on GB10 supports -pm and -lgc. Your workload is mostly decode with heavy prefill bursts on 6-50k prompts with images, so a 2100 MHz cap barely touches decode and costs a little on cold prefill. Prefix caching hides most of that.
kept.risk: Low. If a cap is too low it slows prefill, so do not go below ~1900 MHz unless instability persists. Firmware updates carry the usual small risk. Do them when you can tolerate downtime, and keep the docker images and model cache as they are.
kept.test_plan: (~15 min) Log clocks during one 3-minute mixed load: deep research, then the 11-screenshot Excel job. Then apply the cap and repeat the same load. Compare end-to-end wall time, prefill tok/s and decode tok/s from vLLM logs, peak temperature and power. Accept if decode is within 2% and prefill within 5%.

kept.title: Measure two-engine interference before changing the split, and remove first-request warmup latency after restarts
kept.what_to_change: 1) An idle vLLM engine uses memory but no bandwidth, so an idle Qwen3.8 on :8001 should not slow Gemma. Contention appears only when both decode at once (e.g. Telegram on Gemma plus the Pro model in WebUI): both share ~273 GB/s and each slows. Measure it before deciding anything (see test plan). If the measured slowdown is large and you rarely use Pro, add `--enable-sleep-mode` to the Pro engine and put it to sleep via its `/sleep` endpoint when unused, waking it with `/wake_up`. Sleep-mode endpoints require `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`; check that this works on v0.31 / GB10 before relying on it. 2) Add a warmup to each engine's systemd unit or start script (ExecStartPost: wait for /health, then POST one tiny chat request with max_tokens=3, and for Gemma also one request with a small image). This is so the first real user request after a restart does not pay ~25 s of JIT, compile and graph warmup. 3) Keep `--ipc=host` on both vLLM containers (the vLLM Spark recipe uses it), so the API-server to engine IPC for large multimodal inputs is not limited by Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm.
kept.expected_gain: Warmup: removes a 10-25 s first-request penalty after each restart or deploy, as reported in vLLM's own Spark guide. Interference: no change if both engines are rarely busy at the same time. If they are, the measurement tells you whether sleep mode or routing is worth it. Sleep mode would free roughly 20+ GiB of the Pro engine's weights and KV while it sleeps.
evidence: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-01-vllm-dgx-spark (first request ~25 s JIT; send warmup with max_tokens=3; uses --ipc=host)
https://discuss.vllm.ai/t/2-vllm-containers-on-a-single-gpu/608/2 (memory profiling of the second instance sees the first one's memory)
https://dev.to/ric03uec/two-qwen3-models-on-one-dgx-spark-the-residency-math-for-local-llm-coding-5bpj (two engines on one Spark: sizing/ordering)

https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/running-a-large-llm-on-dgx-spark-cluster-while-keeping-comfyui-usable/376650 (concurrent GPU workloads on Spark slow each other substantially; image gen 5-6x slower under LLM load)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Both engines are vLLM 0.31 on one GB10. I found no published single-user latency benchmark for two co-resident vLLM engines on Spark, so this is a measure-then-decide item. `--enable-sleep-mode` exists in vLLM, but I have not verified that it works with NVFP4 + MTP on sm_121; treat that part as experimental.
kept.risk: Warmup and --ipc=host: very low. Sleep mode: medium. Waking takes several seconds, so the first Pro request after sleep is slower, and there may be bugs on GB10.
kept.test_plan: (~10 min) Gemma benchmark (5x 8k prompt, 512 out) in three states: (a) Qwen container stopped, (b) Qwen running idle, (c) Qwen decoding a long 2k-token answer at the same time. Expect a ≈ b. If c drops more than 30% and you often hit c (check whether Telegram and WebUI Pro overlap), consider sleep mode or routing Telegram away from Pro-time. For warmup: restart Gemma, time the first real user request with and without the ExecStartPost warmup.
